questions.q: What are the five pillars scored separately by the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model?
options: Encryption, Firewalls, Endpoints, Cloud, Compliance
Prevention, Detection, Response, Recovery, Reporting
Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications & Workloads, Data
Perimeter, VPN, MFA, Logging, Patching
questions.explain: The ZTMM scores Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications & Workloads, and Data independently, because a real environment is never uniformly mature and averaging them would hide the gap an attacker would exploit.

questions.q: Why does the CISA ZTMM score the five pillars separately instead of producing one combined zero trust score?
options: Separate scores keep an organization's weakest pillar visible instead of letting strong pillars average out the real gap
A single combined score would require more complex math than agencies can realistically perform
Each pillar belongs to a different vendor's product line, so they can't be combined
CISA requires five separate scores purely for budget-reporting line items
questions.explain: Averaging pillars together would hide exactly the kind of gap an attacker would exploit — an org that's Advanced on Identity but Traditional on Data is not the same risk posture as one that's Initial everywhere, even if the average looks similar.

questions.q: What are the three cross-cutting capabilities that span all five pillars in the ZTMM?
options: Encryption, Authentication, Authorization
Visibility & Analytics, Automation & Orchestration, Governance
Planning, Budgeting, Procurement
Detection, Containment, Eradication
questions.explain: Visibility & Analytics, Automation & Orchestration, and Governance don't belong to any single pillar — they're what make the five pillars work together instead of as five disconnected programs.

questions.q: According to the ZTMM's four maturity stages, what generally changes as an organization moves from Traditional toward Optimal?
options: Nothing changes technically — only the paperwork and audit documentation change
The number of vendors contracted for security tooling increases at each stage
The organization moves from cloud-based controls back to on-premises-only controls
Manual, static, broadly-scoped controls give way to automated, continuously-validated, risk-driven controls
questions.explain: The four stages (Traditional, Initial, Advanced, Optimal) describe a consistent arc from manually configured, statically enforced controls to fully automated, just-in-time, continuously validated access decisions driven by real-time risk signals.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the Traditional → Initial → Advanced progression matters more in practice than Advanced → Optimal?
options: Optimal is not a real stage defined in the published model
Most of an organization's actual risk reduction happens getting to Advanced; Optimal mainly buys speed and scale rather than a fundamentally different risk posture
Advanced and Optimal are scored identically in every pillar
CISA does not expect any organization to ever reach the Advanced stage
questions.explain: The jump from manual/static controls up through Advanced is where most real risk reduction happens; the final move to Optimal is mostly about automation speed and scale at that point, not a different underlying security posture.
